name: Ubaid culture
info: The Ubaid period, c. 6500–3800 BCE, was the prehistoric culture of Mesopotamia that left the earliest known settlements on the southern alluvial plain and spread its painted pottery from Anatolia to the Gulf, before the cities of the Uruk period.

facts.homeland: Mesopotamia (Iraq) and beyond: from Mersin in Turkey to Tepe Ghabristan in Iran and the Gulf coasts of Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE; key sites Tell al-ʿUbaid, Eridu, Ur, Tell el-ʿOueili, Tepe Gawra, Tell Abada, Tell Zeidan, H3
facts.period: c. 6500–3800 BCE in southern Mesopotamia, c. 5300–4300 BCE in the north; divided into phases Ubaid 0–5 (Ubaid 0 at Tell el-ʿOueili c. 6500–6000 BCE); followed by the Uruk period in the south
facts.known: black-on-buff painted pottery; the first temples in Mesopotamia; large unwalled villages of mud-brick houses; ‘ophidian’ figurines; clay boat models and the earliest evidence of seagoing boats and sails; head-shaping and labrets
facts.sources: Excavations from 1919 on (Tell al-ʿUbaid, Eridu, Ur, the Hamrin sites, ʿOueili, Tell Zeidan, Gulf coast sites), pottery sequences, burials, plant and animal remains, a few radiocarbon dates; no writing

t: The Ubaid period left the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian plain, in villages of mud-brick houses with the first temples in Mesopotamia.
Ubaid pottery and customs spread from south-eastern Turkey to the Persian Gulf, according to Gil Stein and Rana Özbal largely through the peaceful spread of ideas rather than conquest.
Graves show growing differences in wealth and rank, but there were still no real cities: those came in the Uruk period that followed.
dyk: A clay disc from the site of H3 in Kuwait shows a two-masted boat, the oldest evidence for the use of masts and sails.
ev: The Ubaid period begins in southern Mesopotamia; Tell el-ʿOueili is the oldest known Ubaid site
Ubaid pottery reaches its peak along the coast of the Persian Gulf
Unalloyed copper pins and chisels are made at Mersin, among the earliest Ubaid metalwork
Central houses grow larger as social differences increase in the late Ubaid
The Ubaid period gives way to the Uruk period in the south
Henry Hall begins the first large excavation of Ubaid material at Tell al-ʿUbaid
A conference in Baghdad defines the ‘Ubaid pottery style’
Joan Oates shows that the Eridu and Hajji Muhammed styles belong to the Ubaid and divides it into phases

sections.origins:
The Ubaid period takes its name from Tell al-ʿUbaid in southern Iraq, where the first large excavation of its material was carried out by Henry Hall in 1919, Leonard Woolley in 1922–1923 and Pinhas Delougaz in 1937. Ubaid pottery was first found at Eridu and Tell al-ʿUbaid in the 1910s and 1920s, and in 1930 a conference in Baghdad defined an “Ubaid pottery style”, a black-on-buff painted ware. Its members wrongly believed that the Eridu and Hajji Muhammed styles were so different that they marked separate “ethnic elements”. In 1960 Joan Oates showed that these styles were part of the wider Ubaid and divided it into four phases; later scholars added two more, so that it is now usually divided into Ubaid 0–5.

In southern Mesopotamia, the land later known as Sumer, the period marks the earliest known settlement of the alluvial plain and runs from about 6500 to 3800 BCE, when the Uruk period followed. Excavations at Tell el-ʿOueili in the 1980s found layers older than those at Eridu and pushed back the date of the first occupation of Lower Mesopotamia; older remains may still lie buried under the river silts. In the north the Ubaid followed the Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf cultures and a short Halaf-Ubaid Transitional period, and lasted only from about 5300 to 4300 BCE. How and when it reached the north is not yet fully understood.

The environment differed from today’s. Wetlands with Euphrates poplar and sea clubrush surrounded ʿOueili in Ubaid 0, date palms grew in the south, and the shoreline of the Persian Gulf moved north until it reached Ur around 4000 BCE. Absolute dates are hard to fix because few radiocarbon dates come from southern Mesopotamia; the sequence rests on the long series of layers at Ur, Eridu and Tepe Gawra.
sections.society:
Ubaid culture is characterised by large unwalled villages, multi-roomed rectangular mud-brick houses and the first temples of public architecture in Mesopotamia. A two-tier pattern of settlement developed, with central sites of more than ten hectares surrounded by villages of less than one. Villages held specialised potters, weavers and metalworkers, although most people were farmers, agricultural labourers and seasonal herders. Excavations in the Hamrin area in the 1970s uncovered a complete Ubaid settlement at Tell Abada and a very well-preserved house at Tell Madhur.

At Tell Zeidan in northern Mesopotamia farmers grew barley, wheat, lentil, ervil and flax, perhaps with floodwater irrigation, and more than 90% of the animal bones came from domesticated sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, compared with about half from wild animals in the earlier Halaf period. In the south, intensive irrigated agriculture and the plough, both introduced from the north, supported farming. On the Gulf coast people fished in shallow waters and even caught tuna. Spindle whorls and changing herds at Kosak Shamali in Syria hint that wool and milk grew in importance towards the late Ubaid.

Graves suggest that society became steadily less equal. Peter Bogucki describes “trans-egalitarian” competitive households, and Morton Fried and Elman Service proposed the rise of hereditary chieftains, perhaps heads of kin groups linked to temple shrines and their granaries. Around 4500–4000 BCE the central houses of settlements became larger, but there were no real cities until the Uruk period. Warfare seems to have been extremely rare: a burnt village at Tell Sabi Abyad and a mass grave of 24 bodies at Tepe Gawra may or may not reflect violence.
sections.beliefs:
No texts survive from the Ubaid period, so ideas about belief rest on buildings, figurines and graves. The period saw the first temples in Mesopotamia, and some scholars link the rising elite to the running of these shrines and their granaries. Most figurines show animals such as sheep, cattle and dogs; most human figurines are female. In the south, “ophidian” figurines, with slender bodies and long, reptile-like heads, became common in the later Ubaid; their faces may represent masks or shaped heads. At first they were used in houses, but in Ubaid 3–4 they also appear in graves, a shift in how they were used.

Most of the dead were buried whole: in Ubaid 4 some 80% of adult and 94% of infant burials were primary inhumations. They were given beads, necklaces and headdresses, pots presumably holding food, and pieces of red ochre. Eridu yielded 193 burials and Tell Abada 127 infant burials. Adults were laid in communal burial grounds at the edge of the settlement, in pits or clay boxes, while infants were buried inside it, often in pots and near larger houses, a pattern that has been linked to growing differences between kin groups. The rarity of ophidian figurines in graves may point to different treatment of the dead by age, kinship or rank.

These customs break clearly with the Late Neolithic, when burials were often secondary and very varied. The move towards whole-body burial and more uniform grave goods has been interpreted as a change in how people understood personhood. Stamp seals, used in Upper Mesopotamia since the seventh millennium BCE, now carried geometric patterns, animals and, for the first time, figures of humans with the heads of ibexes or birds.
sections.arts:
Pottery defines the Ubaid. Painted in black, brown, purple or dark green on a buff to red-green-brown fabric, the wares of Ubaid 1–2 carried dense geometric and abstract decoration, while later pots had simpler bands and swags. The slow potter’s wheel came into use in Ubaid 3–4 and may help explain the plainer decoration. Coarse “coba bowls” from late sites in the north may have been used to hand out rations and may be forerunners of the bevelled-rim bowls of the Uruk period. In the south sickles were often made of hard-fired clay, in the north of stone and sometimes metal.

Flint from the Zagros, Jebel Sinjar and the river terraces was made into arrowheads, sickle blades, drills and the hoes sometimes seen as a hallmark of the Ubaid; good blades may have been made off-site and carried long distances, and production may have passed from households to dedicated craftspeople. Metalworking appears only late and in the north: copper pins and chisels at Mersin about 5000–4900 BCE, furnaces at Değirmentepe and Norşuntepe in Ubaid 3, and copper objects at Tepe Gawra and Tell Arpachiyah. Copper objects are very rare, and no gold has been found at Ubaid sites.

The Ubaid provides the first evidence for boats in the ancient Near East. Clay boat models, more common from Ubaid 3, show reed boats and boats with masts. At H3 in Kuwait a clay disc shows a two-masted boat, the oldest evidence for masts and sails, and lumps of bitumen with barnacles on one side and reed impressions on the other are the earliest evidence for seagoing vessels in the world. People also bound their heads to give them an elongated shape and wore labrets or ear-spools, both perhaps signs of belonging to a group.
sections.exchange:
Ubaid and Ubaid-like material spread over an immense area: from Mersin in the west to Tepe Ghabristan in the east, and from Norşuntepe and Arslantepe in the north to Dosariyah on the Gulf coast of Saudi Arabia. Regional differences are large, and the Ubaid was not one uniform culture through time and space. Gil Stein and Rana Özbal argue that, unlike the colonial expansion of the later Uruk period, the Ubaid expansion took place largely through the peaceful spread of an ideology, with local communities taking up elements of Ubaid material culture and turning them into their own distinct styles.

Along the Persian Gulf, Ubaid pottery appeared towards the end of the sixth millennium BCE, peaked about 5300 BCE and continued into the fifth millennium, at sites such as Bahra 1 and H3 in Kuwait, Dosariyah in Saudi Arabia and Dalma Island in the United Arab Emirates. Local imitations suggest that the pottery itself was traded, perhaps for dates, pearl and shell jewellery, animals or fish. Mesopotamians may have lived part of the year at the Kuwaiti sites, and Arabian Neolithic groups may in turn have lived in southern Mesopotamia, where Arabian Coarse Ware has been found at ʿOueili and Eridu, and flint arrowheads like those of the Arabian Bifacial Tradition at Ur.

Obsidian travelled hundreds of kilometres: tools found at Dosariyah and at Wadi Debayan in Qatar came from south-eastern Turkey. The disappearance of oak from the south during the sixth millennium coincides with the Ubaid’s outward spread, and it has been suggested that the search for good wood helped drive it. Copper may also have been traded, for it lay in elite graves of the Susa I cemetery at Susa, east of the Tigris.
sections.legacy:
In the south the Ubaid gave way about 3800 BCE to the Uruk period, and in the north to the Late Chalcolithic. Archaeologists stress the strong cultural continuity between the Ubaid and Uruk periods: the movement towards urban life began in the Ubaid, with the first temples and a growing elite, though real cities came only later. Some Ubaid customs, such as wearing labrets, declined during the Uruk period, while the coba bowl may foreshadow the Uruk bevelled-rim bowl. Excavations continue to this day; work in Iraqi Kurdistan since the 2010s has shown, for example, that the Shahrizor Plain was more closely tied to the Hamrin area than to the north.

The Ubaid has long featured in the debate called the “Sumerian problem”. Because the oldest cuneiform tablets were written in Sumerian, Henri Frankfort proposed in the 1930s that Sumerian speakers came from the Iranian highlands and settled Mesopotamia at the start of the Ubaid period, while Speiser thought they arrived in the Uruk period and read the earlier Ubaid, Hassuna and Halaf styles as distinct ethnic groups. More recent scholars take care not to equate pots with people, and the languages spoken in the Ubaid period cannot be determined.

Genetics has not yet settled the matter. The few DNA studies of skeletons from Upper Mesopotamia, none of them from the Ubaid period, show both links with other regions and continuity within Mesopotamia, but the genetic influxes they detect cannot yet be dated to the Ubaid or any other earlier period.

summary: The Ubaid period, c. 6500–3800 BCE, was the long prehistoric age that left the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian plain. Its villages of mud-brick houses, first temples, painted pottery and boats spread its influence from south-eastern Turkey to the Persian Gulf, largely without conquest. Graves show growing inequality, but real cities came only in the Uruk period that followed.
